blocks.text: Part of the park on Sorin’s estate. Wide avenue leading away from the spectators into the depths of the park towards the lake is blocked up by a platform roughly put together for private theatricals, so that the lake is not visible. To right and left of the platform, bushes. A few chairs, a little table.
Why do you always wear black?
I am in mourning for my life. I am unhappy.
It isn’t money that matters. A poor man may be happy.

Theoretically, yes; but in practice it’s like this: there are my two sisters and my mother and my little brother and I, and my salary is only twenty-three roubles. We must eat and drink, mustn’t we? One must have tea and sugar. One must have tobacco. It’s a tight fit.

Yes. Miss Zaretchny will act: it is Konstantin Gavrilitch’s play. They are in love with each other and today their souls will be united in the effort to realise the same artistic effect. But your soul and mine have not a common point of contact. I love you. I am so wretched I can’t stay at home. Every day I walk four miles here and four miles back and I meet with nothing but indifference from you. I can quite understand it. I am without means and have a big family to keep.﻿ ﻿… Who would care to marry a man who hasn’t a penny to bless himself with?
Holding out the snuffbox to him.

How stifling it is! There must be a storm coming.﻿ ﻿… You’re always discussing theories or talking about money. You think there is no greater misfortune than poverty, but to my mind it is a thousand times better to go in rags and be a beggar than﻿ ﻿… But you wouldn’t understand that, though.﻿ ﻿…
You imagine your mother does not like your play, and you are already upset and all that. Don’t worry; your mother adores you.
Pulling the petals off a flower.
You can’t do without the stage.
And, by the way, can you tell me, please, what sort of man this literary gentleman is? There’s no making him out. He never says anything.

He is an intelligent man, good-natured and rather melancholy, you know. A very decent fellow. He is still a good distance off forty, but he is already celebrated and has enough and to spare of everything. As for his writings﻿ ﻿… what shall I say? They are charming, full of talent, but﻿ ﻿… after Tolstoy or Zola you do not care to read Trigorin.

Well, I am fond of authors, my boy. At one time I had a passionate desire for two things: I wanted to get married, and I wanted to become an author; but I did not succeed in doing either. Yes, it is pleasant to be even a small author, as a matter of fact.
Oh, it was nothing.﻿ ﻿… You see how out of breath I am. I have to go in half an hour. We must make haste. I can’t stay, I can’t! For God’s sake don’t keep me! My father doesn’t know I am here.
It really is time to begin. We must go and call the others.
I fancy there is someone there.
It’s evening; everything is getting dark. Don’t go away early, I entreat you!
And if I come to you, Nina, I’ll stand in the garden all night, watching your window.
You can’t; the watchman would notice you. Trésor is not used to you, and he would bark.
Take your places. It’s time to begin. Is the moon rising?
Yes, awfully! Your mother is all right﻿—I am not afraid of her﻿—but there’s Trigorin﻿ ﻿… I feel frightened and ashamed of acting before him﻿ ﻿… a celebrated author.﻿ ﻿… Is he young?
It is difficult to act in your play. There are no living characters in it.
Living characters! One must depict life not as it is, and not as it ought to be, but as we see it in our dreams.
It is getting damp. Go back and put on your goloshes.

You don’t take care of yourself. It’s obstinacy. You are a doctor, and you know perfectly well that damp air is bad for you, but you want to make me miserable; you sat out on the verandah all yesterday evening on purpose.﻿ ﻿…
You were so absorbed in conversation with Irina Nikolayevna﻿ ﻿… you did not notice the cold. Own up﻿ ﻿… you are attracted by her.
Nonsense! That’s not old for a man. You look very young for your age, and are still attractive to women.
All you men are ready to fall down and worship an actress, all of you!
Women have always fallen in love with you and thrown themselves on your neck. Is that idealism too?

In the year 1873 she acted marvellously at the fair at Poltava. It was a delight! She acted exquisitely! Do you happen to know, madam, where Pavel Semyonitch Tchadin, a comic actor, is now? His Rasplyuev was inimitable, even finer than Sadovsky’s, I assure you, honoured lady. Where is he now?
There are few actors of brilliant talents nowadays, that’s true; but the average level of acting is far higher than it was.
De gustibus aut bene aut nihil.
In a minute. I beg you to be patient.
“Oh, Hamlet, speak no more! Thou turn’st mine eyes into my very soul; And there I see such black and grained spots As will not leave their tinct.”
And let me wring your heart, for so I shall, If it be made of penetrable stuff.”
A horn is sounded behind the stage.
taps with a stick and recites aloud
There will be nothing in two hundred thousand years.
Then let them present that nothing to us.
In an imploring and reproachful voice.
a pause; two red spots appear upon the background of the lake
There’s a smell of sulphur. Is that as it should be?
The doctor has taken his hat off to the devil, the father of eternal matter.
tries to say something more, but with a wave of his hand goes out on left
Irina, you really must have more consideration for youthful vanity, my dear.
What did I say to him?
He told us beforehand that it was a joke, and I regarded his play as a joke.

Now it appears that he has written a great work. What next! So he has got up this performance and smothered us with sulphur not as a joke but as a protest.﻿ ﻿… He wanted to show us how to write and what to act. This is getting tiresome! These continual sallies at my expense﻿—these continual pinpricks would put anyone out of patience, say what you like. He is a vain, whimsical boy!
He meant to give you pleasure.

Really? He did not choose an ordinary play, however, but made us listen to this decadent delirium. For the sake of a joke I am ready to listen to delirium, but here we have pretensions to new forms and a new view of art. To my thinking it’s no question of new forms at all, but simply bad temper.
Everyone writes as he likes and as he can.
Let him write as he likes and as he can, only let him leave me in peace.
I’ll go and look for him.
Coming out from behind the stage.

Bravo! Bravo! We admired you. With such an appearance, with such a lovely voice, you really cannot stay in the country; it is a sin. You must have talent. Do you hear? It’s your duty to go on the stage.
Who knows? Here, let me introduce Boris Alexyevitch Trigorin.
Making her sit down beside them.
I suppose we may raise the curtain; it’s rather uncanny.
I love angling. There is nothing I enjoy so much as sitting on the bank of a river in the evening and watching the float.
But I should have thought that for anyone who has known the enjoyment of creation, no other enjoyment can exist.
The angel of silence as flown over us.
It’s time for me to go. Goodbye.
Where are you off to? Why so early? We won’t let you go.
If you knew how grieved I am to.
Someone ought to see you home, my little dear.
To her, in an imploring voice.
Stay for an hour. What is there in that?
Shakes hands and hurriedly goes off.

Unfortunate girl she is, really. They say her mother left her father all her immense property﻿—every farthing of it﻿—and now the girl has got nothing, as her father has already made a will leaving everything to his second wife. It’s monstrous!
Yes, her father is a pretty thorough scoundrel, one must do him the justice to say so.
Offering his arm to his wife.
Mashenka is looking for me all over the park. Insufferable creature she is!
Konstantin Gavrilitch, I liked your play extremely. It’s a strange thing, and I haven’t heard the end, and yet it made a strong impression! You are a gifted man﻿—you must persevere.

Fie, what an hysterical fellow! There are tears in his eyes! What I mean is this. You have taken a subject from the realm of abstract ideas. So it should be, for a work of art ought to express a great idea. A thing is only fine when it is serious. How pale you are!
So you tell me to persevere?

Yes.﻿ ﻿… But write only of what is important and eternal. You know, I have had varied experiences of life, and have enjoyed it; I am satisfied, but if it had been my lot to know the spiritual heights which artists reach at the moment of creation, I should, I believe, have despised my bodily self and all that appertains to it and left all things earthly as far behind as possible.

And another thing. In a work of art there ought to be a clear definite idea. You ought to know what is your aim in writing, for if you go along that picturesque route without a definite goal you will be lost and your talent will be your ruin.
But I am going all the same. I must go.
Come indoors, Konstantin Gavrilitch. Your mother wants you. She is worried.
Tell her that I have gone away. And I beg you﻿—all of you﻿—leave me in peace! Let me alone! Don’t follow me about!
Come, come, come, dear boy.﻿ ﻿… You can’t go on like that.﻿ ﻿… That’s not the thing.
Takes her snuffbox from her and flings it into the bushes.
What is it? Help you in what?
Laying her head on his breast, softly.
A croquet lawn. The house with a big verandah in the background on the right, on the left is seen the lake with the blazing sun reflected in it.

There! And why is it? Because I work, I feel I am always on the go, while you stay always in the same place and have no life at all.﻿ ﻿… And it is my rule never to look into the future. I never think about old age or death. What is to be, will be.
walks about the lawn with her arms akimbo
takes the book and looks in it
In a caressing tone, as to a child.
He is in the bathing-house, fishing.
Is about to go on reading.
reads a few lines to herself
You do nothing for your health, brother, and that’s not right.
I should like to take something, but the doctor won’t give me anything.
Even at sixty one wants to live!
It seems to me it would do him good to go to some mineral springs.
Well, he might go. And he might not.
What is one to make of that?
Pyotr Nikolayevitch ought to give up smoking.

No, it’s not nonsense. Wine and tobacco destroy the personality. After a cigar or a glass of vodka, you are not Pyotr Nikolayevitch any more but Pyotr Nikolayevitch plus somebody else; your ego is diffused and you feel towards yourself as to a third person.
One must look at life seriously, but to go in for cures at sixty and to regret that one hasn’t enjoyed oneself enough in one’s youth is frivolous, if you will forgive my saying so.
walks with a lazy, lagging step
She will go and have a couple of glasses before lunch.
She has no personal happiness, poor thing.
You argue like a man who has had all he wants.

Oh, what can be more boring than this sweet country boredom! Hot, still, no one ever doing anything, everyone airing their theories.﻿ ﻿… It’s nice being with you, my friends, charming to listen to you, but﻿ ﻿… to sit in a hotel room somewhere and learn one’s part is ever so much better.
Of course, it’s better in town. You sit in your study, the footman lets no one in unannounced, there’s a telephone﻿ ﻿… in the streets there are cabs and everything.﻿ ﻿…
Yes, we are thinking of it.
Hm! that’s splendid, but how are you going, honoured lady? They are carting the rye today; all the men are at work. What horses are you to have, allow me to ask?
What horses? How can I tell which?
But if I have to go! It’s a queer thing!
Honoured lady! you don’t know what farming means.
People are tiresome. Your husband ought to be simply kicked out, but it will end in that old woman Pyotr Nikolayevitch and his sister begging the man’s pardon. You will see!
I am fifty-five; it’s too late to change my life.
I know you refuse me because there are other women too who are as near to you. You can’t take them all to live with you. I understand. Forgive me, you are tired of me.
I am wretched from jealousy. Of course you are a doctor, you can’t avoid women. I understand.
Irina Nikolayevna is crying and Pyotr Nikolayevitch has an attack of asthma.
Near the house, in a smothered voice.
On receiving them tears the flowers to pieces and throws them away; both go into the house.
Comes in without a hat on, with a gun and a dead seagull.
I was so mean as to kill this bird today. I lay it at your feet.
Picks up the bird and looks at it.
You have so changed, I hardly know you.
Yes, ever since the day when I hardly knew you. You have changed to me, your eyes are cold, you feel me in the way.
lays the seagull on the seat

Good morning. Circumstances have turned out so unexpectedly that it seems we are setting off today. We are hardly likely to meet again. I am sorry. I don’t often have the chance of meeting young girls, youthful and charming; I have forgotten how one feels at eighteen or nineteen and can’t picture it to myself, and so the young girls in my stories and novels are usually false. I should like to be in your shoes just for one hour to find out how you think, and altogether what sort of person you are.
And I should like to be in your shoes.
To know what it feels like to be a famous, gifted author. What does it feel like to be famous? How does it affect you, being famous?
But if you read about yourself in the newspapers?
When they praise me I am pleased, and when they abuse me I feel out of humour for a day or two.

What a wonderful world! If only you knew how I envy you! How different people’s lots in life are! Some can scarcely get through their dull, obscure existence, they are all just like one another, they are all unhappy; while others﻿—you, for instance﻿—you are one out of a million, have an interesting life full of brightness and significance. You are happy.
But surely inspiration and the very process of creation give you moments of exalted happiness?
Forgive me, but I refuse to understand you. You are simply spoiled by success.

What success? I have never liked myself; I dislike my own work. The worst of it is that I am in a sort of delirium, and often don’t understand what I am writing. I love this water here, the trees, the sky. I feel nature, it arouses in me a passionate, irresistible desire to write. But I am not simply a landscape painter; I am also a citizen. I love my native country, my people; I feel that if I am a writer I am in duty bound to write of the people, of their sufferings, of their future, to talk about science and the rights of man and so on, and so on, and I write about everything. I am hurried and flustered, and on all sides they whip me up and are angry with me; I dash about from side to side like a fox beset by hounds. I see life and culture continually getting farther and farther away while I fall farther and farther behind like a peasant too late for the train; and what it comes to is that I feel I can only describe scenes and in everything else I am false to the marrow of my bones.

You are overworked and have not the leisure nor the desire to appreciate your own significance. You may be dissatisfied with yourself, but for others you are great and splendid! If I were a writer like you, I should give up my whole life to the common herd, but I should know that there could be no greater happiness for them than to rise to my level, and they would harness themselves to my chariot.
Covers her face with her hands.
Do you see the house and garden on the other side of the lake?
That house was my dear mother’s. I was born there. I have spent all my life beside this lake and I know every little islet on it.
A seagull. Konstantin Gavrilitch shot it.
makes a note in his book
Advances to the footlights; after a few moments’ meditation.

The dining-room in Sorin’s house. Doors on right and on left. A sideboard. A medicine cupboard. A table in the middle of the room. A portmanteau and hatboxes; signs of preparation for departure. Trigorin is having lunch; Masha stands by the table.

I tell all this to you as a writer. You may make use of it. I am telling you the truth: if he had hurt himself seriously I would not have gone on living another minute. But I have pluck enough all the same. I just made up my mind that I would tear this love out of my heart, tear it out by the roots.
How are you going to do that?
I am going to be married. To Medvedenko.
I don’t understand what’s the object of it.

To love without hope, to spend whole years waiting for something.﻿ ﻿… But when I marry, there will be no time left for love, new cares will smother all the old feelings. And, anyway, it will be a change, you know. Shall we have another?
I don’t want to go myself.
You should beg her to stay.

No, she won’t stay now. Her son is behaving very tactlessly. First he shoots himself, and now they say he is going to challenge me to a duel. And whatever for? He sulks, and snorts, and preaches new forms of art.﻿ ﻿… But there is room for all﻿—new and old﻿—why quarrel about it?
Well, there’s jealousy too. But it is nothing to do with me.

I shall think of you. I shall think of you as you were on that sunny day﻿—do you remember?﻿—a week ago, when you were wearing a light dress﻿ ﻿… we were talking﻿ ﻿… there was a white seagull lying on the seat.
Yes, I shall want them again. You can give away the hooks.
Yes, in my brother’s study, in the corner bookcase.
Really, Petrusha, you had better stay at home.
You are going away; it will be dreary for me at home without you.
And what is there in the town?

What can I say? There were other reasons too. It’s easy to understand; he is young, intelligent, living in the country, in the wilds, with no money, no position and no future. He has nothing to do. He is ashamed of his idleness and afraid of it. I am very fond of him indeed, and he is attached to me, yet in spite of it all he feels he is superfluous in the house, that he is a dependant, a poor relation. It’s easy to understand, it’s amour propre.﻿ ﻿…
Yes, I have money, but you see I am an actress; my dresses alone are enough to ruin me.
goes out leaning on his stick
It is not good for him to live in the country. He gets depressed. If you would be generous for once, mother, and lend him fifteen hundred or two thousand roubles, he could spend a whole year in town.
Mother, change my bandage. You do it so well.
Takes out of the medicine cupboard some iodoform and a box with bandaging material.
He promised to be here at ten, and it is midday already.
takes the bandage off his head
Two ballet dancers lived in the same house as we did at the time.﻿ ﻿… They used to come to you and have coffee.﻿ ﻿…
You don’t understand him, Konstantin. He is a very noble character.﻿ ﻿…
And yet when he was told I was going to challenge him, the nobility of his character did not prevent him from funking it. He is going away. Ignominious flight!
What nonsense! It is I who am asking him to go.

A very noble character! Here you and I are almost quarrelling over him, and at this very moment he is somewhere in the drawing-room or the garden laughing at us﻿ ﻿… developing Nina, trying to convince her finally that he is a genius.
You take a pleasure in saying unpleasant things to me. I respect that man and beg you not to speak ill of him before me.
And I don’t respect him. You want me to think him a genius too, but forgive me, I can’t tell lies, his books make me sick.
That’s envy. There’s nothing left for people who have pretension without talent but to attack real talent. Much comfort in that, I must say!
Tears the bandage off his head.
Get away to your charming theatre and act there in your paltry, stupid plays!
I have never acted in such plays. Let me alone! You are not capable of writing even a wretched burlesque! You are nothing but a Kiev shopman! living on other people!
Walking up and down in agitation.
kisses him on the forehead, on the cheeks and on the head
rapidly puts away the dressings in the cupboard
I hope all your things are packed?
Darling, I know what keeps you here. But have control over yourself. You are a little intoxicated, try to be sober.
I am drawn to her! Perhaps it is just what I need.
The love of a provincial girl? Oh, how little you know yourself!
Sometimes people sleep as they walk﻿—that’s how it is with me, I am talking to you and yet I am asleep and dreaming of her.﻿ ﻿… I am possessed by sweet, marvellous dreams.﻿ ﻿… Let me be free.﻿ ﻿…

If you cared to, you could be not ordinary. Love﻿—youthful, charming, poetical, lifting one into a world of dreams﻿—that’s the only thing in life that can give happiness! I have never yet known a love like that.﻿ ﻿… In my youth I never had time, I was always hanging about the editors’ offices, struggling with want. Now it is here, that love, it has come, it beckons to me. What sense is there in running away from it?
Puts her arms round him and kisses him.

I have no will of my own﻿ ﻿… I have never had a will of my own.﻿ ﻿… Flabby, feeble, always submissive﻿—how can a woman care for such a man? Take me, carry me off, but don’t let me move a step away from you.﻿ ﻿…
In an easy tone as though nothing had happened.
No, we may as well go together.
You are very kind, Polina Andreyevna.
In a greatcoat with a cape to it, with his hat on and a stick in his hand, enters from door on left, crossing the stage.
We humbly thank you, madam! Good journey to you! We are very grateful for your kindness!
May God give you good luck!
You might rejoice our hearts with a letter! Goodbye, Boris Alexeyevitch!
All go out on right. The stage is empty. Behind the scenes the noise that is usual when people are being seen off. The maid comes back to fetch the basket of plums from the table and goes out again.
Between the Third and Fourth Acts there is an interval of two years.

One of the drawing-rooms in Sorin’s house, which has been turned into a study for Konstantin Treplev. On the right and left, doors leading to inner apartments. In the middle, glass door leading on to the verandah. Besides the usual drawing-room furniture there is, in corner on right, a writing-table, near door on left, a sofa, a bookcase and books in windows and on the chairs. Evening. There is a single lamp alight with a shade on it. It is half dark. There is the sound of the trees rustling, and the wind howling in the chimney. A watchman is tapping. Enter Medvedenko and Masha.

How dark it is in the garden! We ought to have told them to break up that stage in the garden. It stands as bare and ugly as a skeleton, and the curtain flaps in the wind. When I passed it yesterday evening, it seemed as though someone were crying in it.
I am sorry for him. He has been three nights now without his mother.
You are a bore. In old days you used at least to discuss general subjects, but now it is only home, baby, home, baby﻿—that’s all one can get out of you.
Your father won’t let me have a horse.
Yes, he will. You ask, and he will.
Very well, I’ll ask. Then you will come tomorrow?
Pyotr Nikolayevitch asked us to make a bed for him in Kostya’s room.
goes up to the writing-table, and leaning on her elbow, looks at the manuscript; a pause
tries to kiss his mother-in-law’s hand
Passes her hand over his hair.
Now you have made him angry. What induced you to pester him?
I feel so sorry for you, Mashenka.
My heart aches for you. I see it all, you know, I understand it all.

It’s all foolishness. There is no such thing as hopeless love except in novels. It’s of no consequence. The only thing is one mustn’t let oneself go and keep expecting something, waiting for the tide to turn.﻿ ﻿… When love gets into the heart there is nothing to be done but to clear it out. Here they promised to transfer my husband to another district. As soon as I am there, I shall forget it all﻿ ﻿… I shall tear it out of my heart.
Two rooms away a melancholy waltz is played.
That’s Kostya playing. He must be depressed.
Noiselessly dances a few waltz steps.
I have six of them at home now. And flour is two kopeks per pound.
You’ve got to look sharp to make both ends meet.
It’s all very well for you to laugh. You’ve got more money than you know what to do with.

Money? After thirty years of practice, my boy, troublesome work during which I could not call my soul my own by day or by night, I only succeeded in saving two thousand roubles, and that I spent not long ago abroad. I have nothing.
With bitter vexation in an undertone.
What changes there have been here! The drawing-room has been turned into a study.
It is more convenient for Konstantin Gavrilitch to work here. Whenever he likes, he can walk out into the garden and think there.
She has gone to the station to meet Trigorin. She will be back directly.
Well, what would you like to have? Valerian drops? Soda? Quinine?
With a motion of his head towards the sofa.
Yes, it’s for you, Pyotr Nikolayevitch.
I wanted to become an actual civil councillor﻿—and I have.
To be expressing dissatisfaction with life at sixty-two is really ungracious, you know.
What a persistent fellow he is! You might understand that one wants to live!
That’s just frivolity. It’s the law of nature that every life must have an end.
You argue like a man who has had enough. You are satisfied and so you are indifferent to life, nothing matters to you. But even you will be afraid to die.

The dread of death is an animal fear. One must overcome it. A rational fear of death is only possible for those who believe in eternal life and are conscious of their sins. And you, in the first place, don’t believe, and, in the second, what sins have you to worry about? You have served in the courts of justice for twenty-five years﻿—that’s all.
We are hindering Konstantin Gavrilitch from working.
Allow me to ask you, doctor, what town did you like best abroad?

The life in the streets is so wonderful there. When you go out of the hotel in the evening, the whole street is packed with people. You wander aimlessly zigzagging about among the crowd, backwards and forwards; you live with it, are psychologically at one with it and begin almost to believe that a world-soul is really possible, such as was acted by Nina Zaretchny in your play. And, by the way, where is she now? How is she getting on?
I expect she is quite well.
I was told that she was leading a rather peculiar life. How was that?
She ran away from home and had an affair with Trigorin. You know that?

She had a child. The child died. Trigorin got tired of her and went back to his old ties, as might have been expected. Though, indeed, he had never abandoned them, but in his weak-willed way contrived to keep both going. As far as I can make out from what I have heard, Nina’s private life was a complete failure.

I fancy that was worse still. She made her debut at some holiday place near Moscow, then went to the provinces. All that time I did not lose sight of her, and wherever she went I followed her. She always took big parts, but she acted crudely, without taste, screamingly, with violent gestures. There were moments when she uttered a cry successfully or died successfully, but they were only moments.
Then she really has some talent?

In the town, staying at an inn. She has been there for five days. I did go to see her, and Marya Ilyinishna here went too, but she won’t see anyone. Semyon Semyonitch declares he saw her yesterday afternoon in the fields a mile and a half from here.
Yes, I saw her. She went in that direction, towards the town. I bowed to her and asked her why she did not come to see us. She said she would come.
walks away with the doctor towards the writing table
She was a charming girl, I say. Actual Civil Councillor Sorin was positively in love with her for a time.
I fancy our people have come back from the station.﻿ ﻿…
You want to bring me ill-luck again, you tiresome man!

Your admirers send their greetings to you.﻿ ﻿… In Petersburg and Moscow there is great interest in your work and I am continually being asked questions about you. People ask what you are like, how old you are, whether you are dark or fair. Everyone imagines, for some reason, that you are no longer young. And no one knows your real name, as you always publish under a pseudonym. You are as mysterious as the Iron Mask.
Will you be able to make a long stay?

No, I think I must go back to Moscow tomorrow. I am obliged to. I am in a hurry to finish my novel, and besides, I have promised something for a collection of tales that is being published. It’s the old story, in fact.

The weather has not given me a friendly welcome. There is a cruel wind. If it has dropped by tomorrow morning I shall go to the lake to fish. And I must have a look at the garden and that place where﻿—you remember?﻿—your play was acted. I’ve got a subject for a story, I only want to revive my recollections of the scene in which it is laid.
Seeing that her father says nothing, waves her hand.
His mother-in-law reluctantly holds out her hand for him to kiss.
goes out with a guilty step
He can walk right enough. He’s not a general.
Turning the pages of the magazine.
puts the magazine down on the writing-table, then goes towards door on left; as he passes his mother he kisses her on the head
The stake is ten kopeks. Put it down for me, doctor, will you?
Has everyone put down their stakes? I begin﻿ ﻿… Twenty-two.
Did you play three? Eight! Eighty-one! Ten!
What a reception I had in Harkov! My goodness! I feel dizzy with it still.
A melancholy waltz is played behind the scenes.
unfastens a brooch on her throat and lays it on the table
I had a wonderful dress.﻿ ﻿… Whatever I don’t know, I do know how to dress.
Kostya is playing the piano; he is depressed, poor fellow.
He is awfully abused in the newspapers.

Ever since I lost you and began to get my work published my life has been unbearable﻿—I am wretched.﻿ ﻿… My youth was, as it were, torn away all at once and it seems to me as though I have lived for ninety years already. I call upon you, I kiss the earth on which you have walked; wherever I look I see your face, that tender smile that lighted up the best days of my life.﻿ ﻿…
I am alone in the world, warmed by no affection. I am as cold as though I were in a cellar, and everything I write is dry, hard and gloomy. Stay here, Nina, I entreat you, or let me go with you!
